mcq.q: The principle that a company is a legal person distinct from its members was firmly laid down in:
options: Ashbury Railway Carriage Co. v. Riche
Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co.
mcq.explain: In Salomon v. Salomon & Co. Ltd. (1897) the House of Lords held that a company validly incorporated is a separate legal person, even if one person holds almost all its shares. Ashbury is the ultra vires case, Turquand the indoor management case, and Carlill a contract-law case on general offers.
mcq.topic: Corporate veil theory and Salomon's case
mcq.fast: Separate entity = Salomon. Ultra vires = Ashbury. Indoor management = Turquand.

mcq.q: A former employee bound by a non-compete covenant forms a company to carry on a competing business, to escape his promise. The court will most likely:
options: Lift the corporate veil and restrain the company, as it is a sham to avoid a legal obligation
Refuse to look behind the company
Treat the company as a partnership firm
mcq.explain: Courts lift the corporate veil when a company is used as a mere cloak or sham to evade legal obligations. In Gilford Motor Co. v. Horne, a former employee who formed a company to escape a restrictive covenant was restrained, along with the company. The separate personality cannot be used to defeat a legal duty.
mcq.fast: Company formed to dodge a legal obligation = sham -> veil lifted (Gilford Motor).

mcq.q: The maximum number of members of a private company, excluding present and certain former employee-members, is:
mcq.explain: Section 2(68) requires a private company's articles to limit the number of its members to 200, except in the case of a One Person Company. Present employees who are members, and former employees who became members while employed and continue after leaving, are not counted. Joint holders are treated as one member.
mcq.topic: Classes by members: OPC, private, small and public companies
mcq.fast: Private company cap = 200 (employees excluded). 50 is the partnership cap.

mcq.q: The minimum number of members required to form a public company is:
mcq.explain: Section 3(1) provides that a company may be formed by seven or more persons for a public company, two or more for a private company, and one person for a One Person Company, by subscribing their names to a memorandum and complying with registration requirements.
mcq.topic: Classes by members: OPC, private, small and public companies
mcq.fast: Public 7, private 2, OPC 1.

mcq.q: Which of the following can incorporate a One Person Company?
options: A minor with his guardian's consent
An individual who is an Indian citizen living in India (resident)
mcq.explain: The Companies (Incorporation) Rules allow only an individual who is both an Indian citizen and an Indian resident to form an OPC or to act as its nominee. A minor cannot be a member or nominee of an OPC. Bodies corporate, Indian or foreign, cannot form an OPC.
mcq.topic: Classes by members: OPC, private, small and public companies
mcq.fast: OPC = natural person + Indian citizen + resident. No companies, no minors.

mcq.q: Helix Ltd holds 45% of the voting power of Nova Ltd but can appoint a majority of Nova's directors. Nova Ltd is:
options: An associate of Helix Ltd only
A subsidiary of Helix Ltd, because Helix controls the composition of its Board
A holding company of Helix Ltd
mcq.explain: Under Section 2(87), Company X is a subsidiary of Company Y if Y decides who sits on X's Board, or if Y commands over half of X's votes. Control over the Board alone is enough, so Nova is a subsidiary even though Helix holds less than half the votes.
mcq.topic: Classes by control and access to capital
mcq.fast: Subsidiary test: Board control OR > 50% voting power — either one is enough.

mcq.q: A company that holds at least 20% of the total voting power of another, but does not control it, has over it a "significant influence". The other company is its:
mcq.explain: Section 2(6) defines an associate company as one in which another company has significant influence, but which is not its subsidiary. Significant influence means holding a fifth or more of the votes, or having a say in its business decisions under an agreement. Joint ventures are also included.
mcq.topic: Classes by control and access to capital
mcq.fast: 20% or more without control = associate. More than 50% or Board control = subsidiary.

mcq.q: A company is a Government company when the Central Government and/or State Governments hold:
options: Not less than 51% of its paid-up share capital
At least 26% of its paid-up share capital
At least 20% of its voting power
mcq.explain: Section 2(45): if the Centre, one or more States, or both together own 51% or more of the paid-up share capital, the company is a Government company. Subsidiaries of such companies are also Government companies.
mcq.topic: Other classes: Government, foreign, Section 8, dormant, Nidhi, PFI
mcq.fast: Government company = 51% or more of paid-up capital with Government(s).

mcq.q: Which statement about a Section 8 company is correct?
options: It applies its profits to promote its objects and is prohibited from paying dividends to members
It must always use "Limited" at the end of its name
It is formed mainly to earn profits for its members
It cannot be formed as a private company
mcq.explain: A Section 8 company exists for non-profit aims — for example the arts, sport, schooling, research, welfare, charity or the environment. It must apply its profits or income to promote these objects and cannot pay dividends. It may be permitted to omit "Limited" or "Private Limited" from its name.
mcq.topic: Other classes: Government, foreign, Section 8, dormant, Nidhi, PFI
mcq.fast: Section 8 = charitable objects + no dividend.

mcq.q: A company formed to hold an intellectual property for a future project, with no significant accounting transactions, may apply to the Registrar for the status of a:
mcq.explain: Section 455 lets a company that was set up for a future project, or simply to hold some asset or IP, and that has no significant accounting activity, ask the Registrar to record it as dormant. It then has to meet only minimal compliance requirements.
mcq.topic: Other classes: Government, foreign, Section 8, dormant, Nidhi, PFI
mcq.fast: Inactive / holding an asset for the future = dormant (s.455).

mcq.q: A private company is a subsidiary of a public company. Under the Companies Act, 2013 it is treated as:
options: A private company in all respects
A public company, even though its articles retain private-company restrictions
mcq.explain: Under the proviso to Section 2(71), a subsidiary of a non-private company is treated as public under the Act, whatever its own articles say, so the stricter public-company rules apply to it. This prevents public companies from escaping rules through private subsidiaries.
mcq.topic: Classes by control and access to capital
mcq.fast: Subsidiary of a public company = deemed public.

mcq.q: A company's directors enter into a contract wholly outside the objects in its memorandum. Later, every shareholder approves it. The contract is:
options: Void, and cannot be ratified even by all the shareholders
Valid if the directors sign again
mcq.explain: Under the doctrine of ultra vires, an act beyond the objects of the memorandum is void from the beginning. In Ashbury Railway Carriage and Iron Co. v. Riche, the House of Lords ruled that no ratification is possible — not even with every shareholder agreeing — because the company never had power to make the contract.
mcq.fast: Ultra vires the company = void, no ratification ever.

mcq.q: Which of these is NOT a clause that must be stated in the memorandum of association under Section 4?
options: The State in which the registered office is situated
The objects for which the company is incorporated
The names of the company's first auditors
mcq.explain: Section 4 requires the memorandum to state the name clause, the State of the registered office, the objects clause, the liability of members, the share capital (for companies having share capital) and, for an OPC, the nominee. The first auditor is appointed by the Board after incorporation and is not part of the memorandum.
mcq.fast: MOA clauses: name, registered office, objects, liability, capital (+ nominee for OPC).

mcq.q: A company issued 4,00,000 shares of ₹10 each, all subscribed, and has called ₹7 per share. Holders of 10,000 shares have not paid the last call of ₹2. Its paid-up capital is:
mcq.explain: Called-up capital = 4,00,000 × ₹7 = ₹28,00,000. Calls in arrears = 10,000 × ₹2 = ₹20,000. Paid-up capital under Section 2(64) is the amount actually paid on shares: ₹28,00,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹27,80,000. ₹40,00,000 is subscribed capital at face value, not paid-up.
mcq.fast: Paid-up = called-up − calls in arrears.

mcq.q: Meena holds 500 shares of ₹10 each, ₹6 paid up, in a company limited by shares. On winding up, her maximum further liability is:
mcq.explain: In a company limited by shares, a member's liability is limited to the amount unpaid on the shares held. Here the unpaid amount is ₹10 − ₹6 = ₹4 per share, so her maximum further liability is 500 × ₹4 = ₹2,000, however large the company's debts may be.
mcq.fast: Liability = shares × unpaid per share.

mcq.q: In a company limited by guarantee, a member's liability arises:
options: Every year, as an annual contribution
Only if he is a director
Only on winding up, up to the amount he undertook in the memorandum
mcq.explain: Section 2(21) defines a company limited by guarantee as one where members' liability is limited by the memorandum to the amount they undertake to contribute to its assets in the event of winding up. The guarantee can therefore be called only on winding up, never during the company's normal life.
mcq.fast: Guarantee company = pay only on winding up, up to the guaranteed sum.

mcq.q: An outsider dealing with a company assumes that the company has completed all its internal formalities, such as passing a required resolution. The doctrine that protects him is:
mcq.explain: Under the doctrine of indoor management, laid down in Royal British Bank v. Turquand, a person dealing with a company in good faith is entitled to assume that its internal procedures have been properly complied with. Constructive notice works the other way, treating outsiders as knowing the contents of the memorandum and articles.
mcq.fast: Internal formalities assumed done = indoor management (Turquand).

mcq.q: Under Section 44, the shares of a company are:
options: Movable property, transferable as the articles lay down
mcq.explain: Section 44 declares a member's shares, debentures and similar interests to be movable property, transferable as the company's articles lay down. That is why shares are also treated as goods under the Sale of Goods Act.
mcq.fast: Shares = movable property (s.44).

mcq.q: How many kinds of share capital does Section 43 recognise?
options: Three kinds — equity, preference and debenture capital
Two kinds — equity share capital and preference share capital
mcq.explain: Section 43 recognises two kinds of share capital: equity share capital (with voting rights, or with differential rights) and preference share capital. Debentures are borrowed money, not share capital, and bonus shares are only a way of issuing equity shares.
mcq.fast: Share capital = equity + preference. Debentures are debt.

mcq.q: Preference shares carry a preferential right as to:
options: Receiving the entire surplus on winding up
Payment of dividend at a fixed rate or amount, and repayment of capital on winding up
mcq.explain: Under the Explanation to Section 43, preference share capital is the part of issued share capital which carries a preferential right to payment of dividend, as a fixed amount or at a fixed rate, and to repayment of capital in a winding up. Preference shareholders generally vote only on matters directly affecting their rights.
mcq.fast: Preference = first claim on dividend + capital refund.

mcq.q: Since the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2015, the common seal of a company is:
options: Optional; without one, two directors (or a director plus the company secretary) sign instead
mcq.explain: The 2015 amendment made the common seal optional. A company may keep one; if it does not, two directors — or a director together with the company secretary, if there is one — sign to authenticate documents. This simplified execution of documents.
mcq.fast: Seal optional since 2015 — two signatures replace it.

mcq.q: A company is called an "artificial person" because:
options: It is created by law and acts only through natural persons such as directors
It exists only on paper and cannot be sued
mcq.explain: A company is a person created by law, not by birth. It can own property, make contracts and sue or be sued in its own name, but it can act only through human agents such as its directors and employees. It cannot be imprisoned, though it can be fined.
mcq.fast: Artificial = created by law + acts through humans.

mcq.q: The registration of a company under Section 9 has the effect that:
options: The company becomes a partnership of its subscribers
The subscribers become personally liable for all debts
The company can never change its name
The subscribers become a body corporate with perpetual succession, able to hold property and to sue and be sued
mcq.explain: Section 9: from the date on the certificate, the subscribers and later members together become a body corporate under the memorandum name, with perpetual succession and the power to own and sell property, make contracts and go to court in that name.
mcq.fast: Registration = birth of a body corporate with perpetual succession.

mcq.q: A company that has any of its securities listed on a recognised stock exchange is called a:
mcq.explain: Under Section 2(52), a company is "listed" if even one class of its securities is traded on a recognised stock exchange. Certain classes of companies that list only specified securities may be excluded by rules. Listing brings extra disclosure obligations under SEBI regulations.
mcq.topic: Classes by control and access to capital
mcq.fast: Securities on a stock exchange = listed.

mcq.q: A company incorporated in Singapore opens a branch office in Mumbai. Under the Companies Act, 2013 it is a:
mcq.explain: Section 2(42) calls a company incorporated abroad a foreign company if it keeps a place of business in India — directly or through an agent, physically or online — and does business here. Such companies must file documents with the Registrar.
mcq.topic: Other classes: Government, foreign, Section 8, dormant, Nidhi, PFI
mcq.fast: Incorporated abroad + place of business in India = foreign company.

mcq.q: Which is NOT a recognised ground on which courts lift the corporate veil?
options: The company is formed to evade taxes
The company is used to avoid a legal obligation
Determining whether a company has enemy character during war
The company has made losses for three years
mcq.explain: Courts have lifted the veil to prevent tax evasion (Dinshaw Maneckjee Petit), to stop the company being used to avoid legal obligations (Gilford Motor), and to determine enemy character (Daimler Co. v. Continental Tyre). Ordinary business losses are not a reason to disregard the company's separate personality.
mcq.fast: Veil lifted for fraud/sham/tax evasion/enemy character — never for mere losses.

mcq.q: A person on whose advice, directions or instructions the Board of Directors is accustomed to act (other than in a purely professional capacity) is treated under Section 2(69) as a:
mcq.explain: Under Section 2(69), a promoter is someone named as promoter in the prospectus or annual return, someone who controls the company's affairs directly or indirectly, or someone whose instructions the Board habitually follows. A person acting only in a professional capacity, such as a lawyer or CA, is excluded.
mcq.fast: Board habitually follows his directions (not as a professional) = promoter.

mcq.q: Assertion (A): A public company can never be a small company.  Reason (R): The definition of small company in Section 2(85) applies only to a company other than a public company.
options: A and R are both true; R does not explain A
A is true; R is false
A and R are both true; R explains A
A is false; R is true
mcq.explain: Both are true and R explains A. Section 2(85) defines a small company as a company other than a public company that meets the prescribed paid-up capital and turnover limits; holding or subsidiary companies, Section 8 companies and companies governed by special Acts are also excluded. A public company is excluded by the definition itself.
mcq.topic: Classes by members: OPC, private, small and public companies
mcq.fast: Small company = private only. R gives the definition that makes A true.
